Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette: John is a 56-year-old male of Oceania ethnicity who works as a detective. He has been divorced for several years and reports experiencing significant distress due to childhood trauma involving physical abuse by his caregiver. John's PTSD symptoms have recently escalated to the point where he is seeking professional help. Growing up, John experienced severe physical abuse at the hands of an adult in his household, which left him with lasting emotional scars. The traumatic event was marked by a burnt smell that still haunts him today and the presence of people who remind him of the victims during those dark times. Over time, these triggers have become increasingly potent, leading John to develop maladaptive strategies such as avoiding wearing similar clothes and detaching himself from his memories. John's avoidance behaviors are intricately tied to his memory fragmentation. Whenever he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread and cannot finish his story. This inability to articulate his experiences has made him feel like a bad coper, further reinforcing his negative beliefs about himself. The intense rage that surges through him when recalling these events makes it nearly impossible for John to maintain a coherent narrative. One of the most distressing aspects is that something in his surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning. These sudden and overwhelming recollections are often triggered by positive emotions, which paradoxically evoke his traumatic past. This trigger-memory cycle has led him to withdraw from social interactions and avoid people who remind him of the victims. The physical reactivity John experiences when reminded of the trauma exacerbates his hypervigilance and sleep vigilance. He is constantly on guard, needing to stay alert at all times. This heightened state of arousal reinforces his negative appraisals about himself and the world around him, making him feel like he is a lousy coper and that something inherent in his character led to these traumatic events. Over time, John's maladaptive strategies have further entrenched his memories and negative beliefs. His avoidance behaviors, such as not wearing certain clothes or isolating himself from others, have made it difficult for him to cope with everyday life. He has come to believe that his reactions since the event show that he is a lousy coper, and this belief intensifies every time he remembers the trauma. John's current state is marked by a profound sense of shattered beliefs about how the world works. His job as a detective often brings him into contact with people who remind him of the victims or situations that trigger his trauma. The stress at work has led to significant interpersonal difficulties, and he has noticed a decline in his ability to perform tasks that once came naturally to him. John's journey toward seeking help was precipitated by an incident where a burnt smell unexpectedly brought back the full memory without warning while he was on duty. This event left him feeling overwhelmed and unable to function effectively at work. His intense fear of being reminded of the trauma, coupled with his growing isolation and inability to cope, finally compelled him to seek professional assistance. John is now most afraid that his past will continue to dominate his present life, making it impossible for him to move forward. He hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to integrate these memories without being consumed by them and regain control over his life.
